title.value: Lombard-VLD: Voice Liveness Detection based on Human Auditory Feedback
Lombard-VLD: Voice Liveness Detection based on Human Auditory Feedback

abstract.value: Voice Liveness Detection (VLD) aims to protect speaker authentication from speech spoofing by determining whether speeches come from live speakers or loudspeakers. Previous methods mainly focus on their differences at the signal level. In this paper, we propose the first VLD that uses the human auditory feedback mechanism (i.e., the Lombard effect), called Lombard-VLD. The key idea is that live speakers can physiologically and involuntarily adjust their speaking patterns in a noisy background but loudspeakers cannot. Moreover, we design a reference-based dual input mode and a differential SE-ResBlock to model the acoustic differences caused by the Lombard effect. Experimental results show that Lombard-VLD achieves 0% and 0.24% EER in two datasets, outperforming the state-of-the-art methods. It is robust to various environmental factors, including different distances, postures of the speaker, and environmental noise, with an average accuracy of over 98.51%. It also has a good generalization to unseen speakers, genders, and datasets, with EER lower than 2.68%, 3.44%, and 7.32%, respectively. This work shows the advantages of the Lombard effect in VLD, which has fewer user limitations and better detection performance.

Voice Liveness Detection (VLD) aims to protect speaker authentication from speech spoofing by determining whether speeches come from live speakers or loudspeakers. Previous methods mainly focus on their differences at the signal level. In this paper, we propose the first VLD that uses the human auditory feedback mechanism ( i.e., the Lombard effect), called Lombard-VLD. The key idea is that live speakers can physiologically and involuntarily adjust their speaking patterns in a noisy background but loudspeakers cannot. Moreover, we design a reference-based dual input mode and a differential SE-ResBlock to model the acoustic differences caused by the Lombard effect. Experimental results show that Lombard-VLD achieves 0% and 0.24% EER in two datasets, outperforming the state-of-the-art methods. It is robust to various environmental factors, including different distances, postures of the speaker, and environmental noise, with an aver- age accuracy of over 98.51%. It also has a good generalization to unseen speakers, genders, and datasets, with EER lower than 2.68%, 3.44%, and 7.32%, respectively. This work shows the advantages of the Lombard effect in VLD, which has fewer user limitations and better detection performance. 1. Introduction Automatic Speaker Verification (ASV) [1], [2], [3], [4], [5] is a technology that analyzes speech signals to iden- tify the speaker. It is a convenient biometric authentication method that eliminates the need for users to remember sen- sitive information such as passwords and PINs. Therefore, ASV is widely used in various fields such as banking, retail finance, judicial forensics, and voice interaction [6]. For example, many mobile applications (e.g., WhatsApp [7] and WeChat [8]) employ ASV for bill payments or login. Unfortunately, ASVs are vulnerable to speech spoofing attacks, such as replay attacks [9], [10], [11] and voice † Hongcheng Zhu and Zongkun Sun contributed equally to this work. ∗ Yanzhen Ren and Kun He are the co-corresponding authors. These attacks broadcast pre-recorded or generated speeches of the target speaker, making it difficult for ASVs to differentiate between genuine and spoofing speeches [22], [23], [24], [25], leading to illegal access and property losses. For instance, spoofing speeches have been known to fool the ASV systems used by the Australian Tax Office [26] and some banks [27], [28]. V oice Liveness Detection (VLD) is a common technique to defend against speech spoofing attacks by determining whether the current speech comes from a live person or a loudspeaker. Existing methods adopt a one-pass paradigm, which analyzes a piece of speech at the signal level, by detecting liveness feedback characteristics associated with that speech ( e.g., human movements and vibrations) via the device's loudspeaker [29], [30], [31], [32], [33] or additional sensors [34], [35], [36], [37], [38], [39], [40], or by an- alyzing vocal differences between live speakers and loud- speakers [41], [42], [43], [44], [45], [46]. However, these one-pass methods are typically limited by user posture and distance, lack sufficient robustness in noisy environments or user movements, and rarely consider generalization across unknown speakers, genders, and datasets. Therefore, they perform poorly in practice. 4303 DOI 10.1109/SP61157.2025.00226 In this paper, we propose the Lombard-VLD framework, which adopts a two-pass VLD paradigm and achieves more accurate, relatively convenient, robust, and generalized voice liveness detection. This framework identifies live speakers from two pieces of correlated speech based on their physio- logical conditioned reflex known as the Lombard effect [47], [48], [49], where live speakers adjust their speaking patterns in response to background noise to enhance communication clarity. The Lombard effect, controlled by the human cortical network, is highly robust and difficult to suppress even with instructions [50], [51], [52], making it suitable for voice liveness detection. However, the application of the Lombard effect in VLD also faces two significant challenges. C1: How to model the features related to the Lombard effect in a robust and universal manner? Previous work [53], [54], [55], [56], [57], [58], [59], [60], [61] qualitatively analyzed some Lombard-related acoustic features, such as loudness, pitch, F1 (first formant frequency), and alpha ratio (energy ratio between 50-1000Hz and 1-15kHz). However, these features are highly speaker-dependent and can also vary with the speech content and the background noise level. C2: There is no dataset suitable for real-world scenarios. The existing Mandarin Lombard corpus (DB-MLC) [60] was recorded in a quiet studio and did not take into account various envi- ronment interference factors, such as multiple device types, distance, angles, and environment noise levels. However, we urgently need a new dataset that involves these factors to study whether Lombard effect-based voice liveness detection can be applied to real-world environments. To solve C1, we first analyze why live speakers can respond to background noise while loudspeakers cannot, and the acoustic feature changes caused by the Lombard effect of live speakers. Then, we design a reference-based dual input mode and a differential SE-ResBlock to model the Lombard- related differential features, as shown in Figure 1. These designs enable Lombard-VLD to ignore the same factors in two inputs as much as possible (such as speaker identity and content) and focus more on modeling the feature differences brought about by the Lombard effect, thus empowering our framework with robustness and generalization. To solve C2, we have made a new multi-factor Mandarin Lombard corpus (DB-MMLC) that involves various environment interference factors to evaluate the feasibility of Lombard-VLD in real- world applications. Experimental results show that Lombard-VLD achieves 100.00% and 99.76% iEER ( i.e., inverse EER, iEER = 1 - EER) on DB-MLC [60] and DB-MMLC datasets, re- spectively. Additionally, Lombard-VLD exhibits robustness, achieving an average of 99.41% iEER even when exposed to various environmental interference factors. It also has gen- eralization, achieving at least 97.32%, 96.56%, and 92.68% iEER in unseen speakers, genders, and datasets, respectively. More importantly, Lombard-VLD can defend various speech spoofing attacks with at least 97.36% iEER. Since Lombard- VLD utilizes the Lombard effect of live speakers, it does not rely on additional sensors, nor requires users to keep specific postures and distances. To summarize, our contributions are as follows. • We propose the Lombard-VLD framework which uses speakers' changes in speaking patterns for voice liveness detection. To our knowledge, it is the first approach to use the human auditory feedback mech- anism in VLD. A comparison of related work is shown in TABLE 1. • To improve the robustness and generalization across different speakers, speech contents, and background noise levels, we design a reference-based dual input mode and a differential SE-ResBlock. • To evaluate the effectiveness of our framework in real-world applications, we create a new multi-factor Mandarin Lombard corpus (DB-MMLC) that in- volves various environmental factors. • Lombard-VLD has four advantages: 1) Low cost and do not require users to keep specific postures or distance; 2) High detection accuracy , i.e., it can identify live speakers with 100% and 99.76% iEER in DB-MLC and DB-MMLC; 3) High robustness, i.e., it is robust to various environment interference factors; 4) High generalizability, i.e., it can gener- alize to the unseen speaker, gender, and even dataset. 2. Related Work Speech Spoofing. This technology can deceive ASV systems by playing pre-recorded or generated speeches through loudspeakers, potentially leading to unauthorized access to target user privileges. Currently, there are two main categories of speech spoofing methods: replay attacks and voice deepfake attacks. The former [9], [10], [11] plays back the secretly recorded real voices of the target user through loudspeakers. The latter [12], [13], [14], [15], [16], [17], [17], [18], [19], [20], [21] generates spoofing speeches that possess the target user's timbre and speaking style.
